---
title: "Generator"
subtitle: "The families -C/-D/-E/-W, the scale options, and the instances they build"
---

Without `-d`, `zeno` builds the instance with the generator of the 2016 solvers, from the options
`-n -t -p -C -D -E -W -r -j -k -l -m -x -y` ([command line](../solver/cli.qmd#instance-options)).
The construction is that of `legacy::buildInstance` (`src/zeno/legacy_input.cpp`), quirks
included, so `zeno` and the 2016 `zenoSolver` see the same instance for the same options.

## Generating functions

`-C`, `-D`, `-E` and `-W` each take a code:

| Code | Function $f(k)$ | Name in the suites |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $\ln k$ | `log` |
| 2 | $\sqrt k$ | `sqrt` |
| 3 (default) | $k$ | `linear`, identity |
| 4 | $2^k$ | `pow2` |
| 5 | $5\lfloor k/2 \rfloor + 0.1\,(k \bmod 2)$ | `staircase`, the "(5/2)$i$" family |

Any other code falls back to the identity, as in 2016. The argument $k$ is truncated to an unsigned
integer before $f$ is applied, as the 2016 functions took `unsigned`.

## Construction

For cities $i = 1, \dots, n$, with $r$ = `-r`, $(j, k)$ = `-j -k`, $(l, m)$ = `-l -m` and $(x, y)$ =
`-x -y` (defaults $r = 1$, $j = l = x = 1$, $k = m = y = 0$):

1. Costs on increasing arguments, durations on **decreasing** ones:
   $$c_i = x\,f_C(\lfloor j\,i + k \rfloor) + y, \qquad d_i = x\,f_D(\lfloor l\,(n+1-i) + m \rfloor) + y.$$
   With `-E` and `-W` (both needed; `-D` is then ignored), $d_i$ uses $f_E$ and the $C_G$-side
   $\bar d_i = x\,f_W(\lfloor l\,(n+1-i) + m \rfloor) + y$.
2. Every value is multiplied by $r$ and truncated toward zero: $v \leftarrow \operatorname{trunc}(r\,v)$.
   `-r 100` keeps slowly growing functions such as $\ln$ from collapsing onto a few integers.
3. **The swap.** If $d_1 > d_2$, durations and costs are exchanged and $\bar d$ is reversed
   ([model](model.qmd#swap)). For increasing functions on decreasing arguments $d_1 > d_2$ holds
   unless truncation makes the first two values equal. So in practice:

| Options | Swap? | Durations $d_i$ | $C_G$ side $\bar d_i$ | Costs $c_i$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `-C a -D b` | yes (usual) | $\operatorname{trunc}(r\,(x f_a(ji+k)+y))$ | $= d_i$ | $\operatorname{trunc}(r\,(x f_b(l(n+1-i)+m)+y))$ |
| `-C a -D b` | no (tie) | $\operatorname{trunc}(r\,(x f_b(l(n+1-i)+m)+y))$ | $= d_i$ | $\operatorname{trunc}(r\,(x f_a(ji+k)+y))$ |
| `-C a -E e -W w` | yes (usual) | $\operatorname{trunc}(r\,(x f_a(ji+k)+y))$ | $\operatorname{trunc}(r\,(x f_w(li+m)+y))$ | $\operatorname{trunc}(r\,(x f_e(l(n+1-i)+m)+y))$ |
| `-C a -E e -W w` | no (tie) | $\operatorname{trunc}(r\,(x f_e(l(n+1-i)+m)+y))$ | $\operatorname{trunc}(r\,(x f_w(l(n+1-i)+m)+y))$ | $\operatorname{trunc}(r\,(x f_a(ji+k)+y))$ |

(the floors inside $f$ are left out for readability). After the usual swap, durations increase
with $i$ and costs decrease: faster cities cost more, which is what makes the front non-trivial.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Non-symmetric options that give a symmetric instance

After the swap, the $C_I$-side durations come from `-C` and the $C_G$-side ones from `-W`. When the
two functions coincide the instance is **symmetric**, whatever `-E` says. `-n 3 -E 1 -W 3` (with
the default `-C 3`) is symmetric, and `zeno` solves it as such. Use a `-W` different from `-C`,
for example `-E 3 -W 2`:

```text
$ zeno generate -n 4 -t 3 -p 2 -E 3 -W 2 -r 10
10 20 30 40
10 14 17 20
40 30 20 10
```
:::

## Examples

These are the outputs of `zeno generate` (durations, then costs; 3 lines when non-symmetric):

| Options | Instance |
|---|---|
| `-n 4` (defaults, linear) | $d = (1, 2, 3, 4)$, $c = (4, 3, 2, 1)$ |
| `-n 4 -C 2 -D 2 -r 10` | $d = (10, 14, 17, 20)$, $c = (20, 17, 14, 10)$ |
| `-n 10 -D 1 -r 100` | $d = (100, 200, \dots, 1000)$, $c = (230, 219, 207, 194, 179, 160, 138, 109, 69, 0)$ |
| `-n 10 -D 1` (tie: no swap) | $d = (2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0)$, $c = (1, 2, \dots, 10)$ |
| `-n 4 -E 3 -W 2 -r 10` | $d = (10, 20, 30, 40)$, $\bar d = (10, 14, 17, 20)$, $c = (40, 30, 20, 10)$ |

Zero values are allowed and do occur: $\ln 1 = 0$, so the log family has a city of duration or
cost 0.

## The families in the suites

The `families` suite runs every family on $n = 10$, $t = 8$, $p = 3$
([suites](suites.qmd#suite-families)): `linear` (`-C 3 -D 3`), `log` (`-C 1 -D 1 -r 100`), `sqrt`
(`-C 2 -D 2 -r 100`), `pow2` (`-C 4 -D 4`), `staircase` (`-C 5 -D 5 -r 10`), and the mixed
`log-linear` and `sqrt-linear`. The default family is the only one with a closed-form front
([known fronts](known-fronts.qmd)). The others need the general algorithm, and on them the 2016
greedy can miss points.

Every instance the generator builds without `-E`/`-W` is symmetric, and every PDDL problem `zeno`
writes from it satisfies (A1), so its front is exact.
